n: A few days after calling His first disciples, Jesus attends a wedding in Cana, a Galilean village near Nazareth. His mother Mary is there too, perhaps helping the family.

f.g: Probably counted from the last event in chapter 1.
A village a few miles north of Nazareth; Nathanael’s hometown.

n: Jesus and His new disciples have also been invited. His first miracle takes place at a joyful family celebration.

f.g: Invited.

n: The wine runs out — a serious embarrassment for the host family, since village weddings lasted up to a week and hospitality was a matter of honor. Mary turns to Jesus.

f.g: Ran short of wine.

n: Jesus’ reply sounds abrupt in English, but “Woman” was a respectful address. The JST renders it: “Woman, what wilt thou have me to do for thee? that will I do; for mine hour is not yet come.”

f.g: A polite, even honorable, form of address — Jesus uses it from the cross too.

f.w: mine hour is not yet come
f.g: His “hour” in John points to His death and glorification.

n: Mary’s faith is clear. She tells the servants: whatever He tells you, do it. That counsel still applies to every disciple.

f.w: Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it

n: Six large stone jars stand nearby, used for ritual hand-washing under Jewish purity customs. Each holds about twenty to thirty gallons.

f.g: Stone vessels were believed not to become ritually impure, unlike clay.
A measure of about 9–10 gallons; each jar held 20–30 gallons.

n: Jesus tells the servants to fill the jars with water, and they fill them to the very brim — leaving no room for anything to be added.

f.g: Completely full — no trickery possible.

n: He tells them to draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet, and they obey — trusting before seeing.

f.g: The head steward or master of ceremonies at the feast.

n: The banquet master tastes the water that has become wine. He doesn’t know where it came from, but the servants who obeyed do. He calls over the groom.

f.w: the servants which drew the water knew
f.g: Those who obey are often the first to witness God’s works.

n: He tells the groom: normally the best wine is served first and the cheaper wine later. But you’ve saved the best for last! Christ’s gifts surpass what came before.

f.g: Drunk freely.

f.w: thou hast kept the good wine until now
f.g: Many see a symbol: the new covenant surpasses the old.

n: This was the first of Jesus’ “signs,” revealing His glory, and His disciples believed in Him. John calls miracles “signs” because they point to who Jesus is.

f.g: Literally “beginning of signs” — John records seven signs.

n: Afterward, Jesus goes down to Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee with His mother, brothers, and disciples, staying a few days.

f.g: A lakeside town that became Jesus’ base in Galilee.

n: With Passover approaching, Jesus goes up to Jerusalem. John’s Gospel mentions three Passovers, which is why we think Jesus’ ministry lasted about three years.
In the temple courts He finds merchants selling cattle, sheep, and doves for sacrifice, and moneychangers at their tables. A place of prayer has become a bustling market.

f.g: They exchanged foreign coins for the Tyrian shekels required for the temple tax — often at a profit.

n: He makes a whip from cords and drives them out with their animals, scattering the money and overturning the tables. Only John places a cleansing at the start of the ministry; the other Gospels describe one in the final week.

f.g: A whip made of rushes or rope.

n: To the dove sellers He says: get these out of here! Don’t turn My Father’s house into a marketplace. Calling the temple “My Father’s house” is a bold claim to be God’s Son.
His disciples remember a line from the Psalms: zeal for God’s house will consume Him. His passion for the temple would indeed help lead to His death.

f.w: The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up

n: The authorities demand a miraculous sign to prove He has authority to do this.
Jesus answers cryptically: destroy this temple, and I will raise it up in three days. His sign will be His own resurrection.
They take Him literally. Herod’s rebuilding of the temple had been going on for forty-six years — how could He rebuild it in three days?

f.g: Herod began rebuilding about 20/19 BC, which helps date this event to about AD 27–28; work continued until AD 63.
Raise it up, build it.

n: John explains: He was speaking of the temple of His body. His body is the true dwelling place of God.
After the Resurrection, the disciples remembered this and believed both the scriptures and Jesus’ words. Some understanding comes only later.
During the Passover feast in Jerusalem, many believed in Him because of the miracles they saw.

f.g: Their belief was based on seeing signs — a beginning, but shallow.

n: But Jesus didn’t entrust Himself to them, because He knew everyone’s heart. Faith built only on wonders can be fickle.

f.g: Entrust Himself — same Greek word as “believed” in v. 23, a wordplay.

n: He needed no one to tell Him about people, for He knew what was in each person. Nothing is hidden from Him.

f.w: he knew what was in man
